title: II. The Injured Foot
paragraphs: The first of these errands was at Madame Hohlakov's house, and he hurried there to get it over as quickly as possible and not be too late for Mitya. Madame Hohlakov had been slightly unwell for the last three weeks: her foot had for some reason swollen up, and although she wasn't bedridden, she lay all day half-reclining on the couch in her boudoir in a fascinating but decorous _déshabillé_. Alyosha had once noted with innocent amusement that in spite of her illness Madame Hohlakov had begun to be rather dressy — top-knots, ribbons, loose wrappers had appeared, and he had an inkling of the reason, though he dismissed such thoughts as frivolous. Over the last two months the young official Perhotin had become a regular visitor at the house.

Alyosha hadn't called for four days, and he was in a hurry to go straight to Lise, since it was with her that he needed to speak; Lise had sent a maid to him the day before, specifically asking him to come to her “about something very important” — a request which, for certain reasons, was of interest to Alyosha. But while the maid went to take his name in to Lise, Madame Hohlakov heard from someone that he had arrived, and immediately sent word begging him to come to her “for just one minute.” Alyosha decided it was better to accede to mamma's request, or else she would keep sending down to Lise's room every other minute while he was there. Madame Hohlakov was lying on a couch. She was particularly smartly dressed and was clearly in a state of extreme nervous excitement. She greeted Alyosha with cries of delight.

“It's ages, ages, absolute ages since I've seen you! A whole week — think of it! Ah, but you were here only four days ago, on Wednesday. You've come to see Lise. I'm sure you meant to slip into her room on tiptoe without my hearing. My dear, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, if you only knew how worried I am about her! But that later — though it is the most important thing, that later. Dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, I trust you with my Lise utterly. Since the death of Father Zossima — God rest his soul!” (she crossed herself) “— I look on you as a monk, though you look charming in your new suit. Where did you find such a tailor in these parts? No, no, that isn't the main thing — that later. Forgive me for sometimes calling you Alyosha; an old woman like me may take liberties,” she smiled coquettishly. “But that later too. The important thing is that I mustn't forget what's important. Please remind me of it yourself. As soon as my tongue runs away with me, you just say, ‘the important thing?' Ach — how do I know now what is most important? Ever since Lise took back her promise — her childish promise, Alexey Fyodorovitch — to marry you, of course you've realized it was only the playful fancy of a sick child who had been so long confined to her chair — thank God, she can walk now! — that new doctor Katya sent for from Moscow for your unhappy brother, who tomorrow — But why speak of tomorrow? I'm ready to die at the very thought of tomorrow. Ready to die of curiosity. That doctor was with us yesterday and saw Lise. I paid him fifty roubles for the visit. But that's not the point, that's not the point again. You see, I'm mixing everything up. I'm in such a hurry. Why am I in a hurry? I don't know. It's dreadful how I seem to be losing my grip on everything. Everything seems mixed up in a sort of tangle. I'm afraid you're so bored you'll jump up and run away, and that will be all I see of you. Goodness! Why are we sitting here and no coffee? Yulia, Glafira, coffee!”
Alyosha hurried to thank her and said he had only just had coffee.
“Where?”
“At Agrafena Alexandrovna's.”

“At ... that woman's? Ah, she's the one who has brought ruin on everyone. Though I know nothing about it. They say she has turned into a saint — though rather late in the day. She ought to have done it before. What use is it now? Hush, hush, Alexey Fyodorovitch, for I have so much to say to you that I'm afraid I won't say any of it. This awful trial ... I'll certainly go, I'm making arrangements. I'll be carried there in my chair; besides, I can sit up. I'll have people with me. And, you know, I'm a witness. How am I to speak, how am I to speak? I don't know what I'll say. One has to take an oath, doesn't one?”
“Yes; but I don't think you'll be able to go.”

“I can sit up. Ah, you put me out! Ah — this trial, this savage business, and then they're all going off to Siberia, some are getting married, and all this so quickly, so quickly, everything changing, and in the end — nothing. Everyone grows old and has nothing to look forward to but death. Well, so be it! I'm weary. This Katya, _cette charmante personne_, has disappointed all my hopes. Now she's going to follow one of your brothers to Siberia, and your other brother is going to follow her, and live in the nearest town, and they'll all torment each other. It drives me out of my mind. Worst of all — the publicity. The story has been told a million times in all the papers in Moscow and Petersburg. Ah, yes — would you believe it, there's a paragraph saying I was ‘a dear friend' of your brother's ——, I can't repeat the horrid word. Just imagine, just imagine!”
“Impossible! Where was the paragraph? What did it say?”

“I'll show you right away. I got the paper and read it yesterday. Here — in the Petersburg paper _Gossip_. The paper began publishing this year. I'm awfully fond of gossip, and I subscribe, and now it pays me back — this is what gossip comes to! Here it is, here, this passage. Read it.”
And she handed Alyosha a sheet of newspaper that had been tucked under her pillow.

It wasn't exactly that she was upset — she seemed overwhelmed, and perhaps everything really was mixed up in a tangle in her head. The paragraph was very typical, and must have been a great shock to her, but, fortunately perhaps, she was unable at that moment to keep her mind fixed on any one subject, and so might race off a minute later to something else and forget the newspaper altogether.

Alyosha was well aware that the story of the terrible case had spread all over Russia. And, good heavens — what wild rumors about his brother, about the Karamazovs, and about himself he had read in the course of those two months, among other equally credible items! One paper had even reported that he had entered a monastery and taken the cowl in horror at his brother's crime. Another contradicted this and said that he and his elder, Father Zossima, had broken into the monastery strongbox and “made tracks from the monastery.” The present paragraph in the paper _Gossip_ appeared under the heading “The Karamazov Case at Skotoprigonyevsk.” (That, alas, was the name of our little town. I had so far kept it concealed.) It was brief, and Madame Hohlakov was not directly mentioned in it. No names appeared at all, in fact. It merely stated that the criminal, whose forthcoming trial was causing such a sensation — retired army captain, idle swaggerer, and reactionary bully — was constantly involved in amorous intrigues and particularly popular with certain ladies “who were pining in solitude.” One such lady, a pining widow who tried to look young though she had a grown daughter, was so fascinated by him that only two hours before the crime she had offered him three thousand roubles on condition that he elope with her to the gold mines. But the criminal, counting on escaping punishment, had preferred to murder his father for the three thousand rather than go off to Siberia with the middle-aged charms of his pining lady. This playful paragraph concluded, of course, with an outburst of generous indignation at the wickedness of parricide and at the recently abolished institution of serfdom. Reading it with curiosity, Alyosha folded up the paper and handed it back to Madame Hohlakov.

“Well, that must be me,” she hurried on again. “Of course I'm the one meant. Scarcely more than an hour before, I'd suggested gold mines to him, and here they talk of ‘middle-aged charms' as if that were my motive! He writes that out of spite! God Almighty forgive him for the middle-aged charms, as I forgive him! You know it's — Do you know who it is? It's your friend Rakitin.”
“Perhaps,” said Alyosha, “though I've heard nothing about it.”
“It's him, it's him! No ‘perhaps' about it. You know I turned him out of the house. You know the whole story, don't you?”
“I know you asked him not to visit you in the future, but why, exactly, I haven't heard ... at least, not from you.”
“Ah, then you've heard it from him! He abuses me, I suppose? Abuses me dreadfully?”
“Yes, he does; but then he abuses everyone. But why you've given him up, I haven't heard from him either. I see him very seldom these days, in fact. We're not friends.”

“Well, then, I'll tell you all about it. There's no help for it — I'll confess, because there's one point in which I was perhaps to blame. Only a little, little point, so small it may not even count. You see, my dear boy” — Madame Hohlakov suddenly looked arch, and a charming though enigmatic smile played over her lips — “you see, I suspect ... You must forgive me, Alyosha. I'm like a mother to you. No, no — quite the contrary. I speak to you now as though you were my father — mother is quite out of place. Well, it's as though I were confessing to Father Zossima, that's just it. I called you a monk just now. Well, that poor young man, your friend, Rakitin (Mercy on us! I can't be angry with him. I feel cross, but not very), that frivolous young man, would you believe it, seems to have taken it into his head to fall in love with me. I only noticed it later. At first — a month ago — he just started dropping in more often, almost every day, though, of course, we'd been acquainted before. I knew nothing about it ... and then suddenly it dawned on me, and I began noticing things with surprise. You know, two months ago that modest, charming, excellent young man Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, who works here in the service, began coming regularly. You've met him here any number of times yourself. And he's an excellent, earnest young man, isn't he? He comes once every three days, not every day (though I'd be glad to see him every day), and always so well dressed. Altogether, Alyosha, I love young people — talented, modest, like you — and he has almost the mind of a statesman, he speaks so charmingly, and I'll most certainly, certainly try to get him promotion. He's a future diplomat. On that dreadful day he almost saved me from death by coming in the night. And your friend Rakitin comes in such boots, and always stretches them out across the carpet. Anyway, he began hinting at his feelings, and one day as he was leaving he squeezed my hand terribly hard. My foot began to swell directly after he pressed my hand like that. He had met Pyotr Ilyitch here before, and would you believe it, he's always gibing at him, growling at him for some reason. I just watched the way they went on together and laughed to myself. So I was sitting here alone — no, I was laid up by then. Well, I was lying here alone, and suddenly in comes Rakitin, and — imagine! — he brought me some verses of his own composition, a short poem, on my bad foot; that is, he had described my foot in a poem. Wait a minute — how did it go?
A captivating little foot.

It began something like that. I can never remember poetry. I've got it here. I'll show it to you later. But it's a charming thing — charming — and, you know, it's not only about the foot, it had a good moral too, a charming idea, only I've forgotten it; in fact, it was just the thing for an album. So, of course, I thanked him, and he was clearly flattered. I'd hardly finished thanking him when in comes Pyotr Ilyitch, and Rakitin suddenly looked as black as night. I could see that Pyotr Ilyitch was in the way, because Rakitin had certainly wanted to say something after giving me the verses. I had a presentiment of it; but Pyotr Ilyitch came in. I showed Pyotr Ilyitch the verses without saying who was the author. But I'm convinced he guessed, though he won't own it to this day and insists he had no idea. He only says that on purpose. Pyotr Ilyitch immediately began to laugh and set to criticizing it. ‘Wretched doggerel,' he said they were, ‘some divinity student must have written them,' and with such vehemence, such vehemence! Then, instead of laughing, your friend flew into a rage. ‘Good gracious,' I thought, ‘they'll fly at each other.' ‘I wrote them,' he said. ‘I wrote them as a joke,' he said, ‘for I think it degrading to write verses. But they are good poetry. They want to put up a monument to your Pushkin for writing about women's feet, while I wrote with a moral purpose, and you,' he said, ‘are an advocate of serfdom. You've no humane ideas,' he said. ‘You have no modern enlightened feelings, you're untouched by progress, you're a mere pen-pusher,' he said, ‘and you take bribes.' Then I began screaming and imploring them. And Pyotr Ilyitch is anything but a coward, you know. He at once took up the most gentlemanly tone, looked at him sarcastically, listened, and apologized. ‘I'd no idea,' he said. ‘I wouldn't have said it if I had known. I'd have praised it. Poets are all so irritable,' he said. In short, he laughed at him under cover of the most gentlemanly tone. He explained to me afterwards that it had all been sarcastic. I'd thought he was in earnest. But as I lay there, just as before you now, I was thinking, ‘Would it, or would it not, be the proper thing for me to turn Rakitin out for shouting so rudely at a visitor in my house?' And, would you believe it, I lay here, shut my eyes, and wondered, would it be the proper thing or not. I fretted and fretted, and my heart began to beat, and I couldn't make up my mind whether to make a scene or not. One voice seemed to be telling me, ‘Speak,' and the other, ‘No, don't speak.' And no sooner had the second voice said that than I cried out, and fainted. Of course, there was a fuss. I got up suddenly and said to Rakitin, ‘It's painful for me to say it, but I don't wish to see you in my house again.' So I turned him out. Ah, Alexey Fyodorovitch — I know myself that I did wrong. I was putting it on. I wasn't really angry with him at all; but I suddenly imagined — that was what did it — that it would be such a fine scene. And yet, believe me, it turned out quite natural, because I actually did shed tears and cried for several days afterwards, and then suddenly one afternoon I forgot all about it. So it's been a fortnight since he's been here, and I kept wondering whether he'd come again. I was even wondering yesterday, and then last night this _Gossip_ appeared. I read it and gasped. Who could have written it? He must have written it. He went home, sat down, wrote it on the spot, sent it off, and they printed it. It was a fortnight ago, you see. But Alyosha, it's awful how I keep talking and don't say what I want to say. Ah — the words come of themselves!”
“It's very important to me to get to my brother on time today,” Alyosha faltered.
“To be sure, to be sure! You bring it all back to me. Listen — what is an aberration?”
“What aberration?” Alyosha asked, wondering.
“In the legal sense. An aberration in which everything is pardonable. Whatever you do, you'll be acquitted right away.”
“What do you mean?”

“I'll tell you. This Katya ... Ah, she's a charming, charming creature, only I can never make out who it is she's in love with. She was here with me some time ago and I couldn't get anything out of her. Especially since she won't talk to me about anything but surface matters now. She's always talking about my health, and nothing else, and she takes up such a tone with me, too. I simply said to myself, ‘Well, so be it. I don't care.' Oh yes — I was talking about aberration. This doctor has come. You know the doctor has come? Of course, you know — the one who diagnoses madmen. You sent for him. No, it wasn't you, it was Katya. It's all Katya's doing. Well, you see — a man may be sitting there perfectly sane and suddenly have an aberration. He may be conscious and know what he's doing, and yet be in a state of aberration. And there's no doubt Dmitri Fyodorovitch was suffering from aberration. They discovered aberration as soon as the courts were reformed. It's all thanks to the reformed courts. The doctor was here and questioned me about that evening, about the gold mines. ‘How did he seem then?' he asked. He must have been in a state of aberration. He came in shouting, ‘Money, money, three thousand! Give me three thousand!' and then went away and immediately did the murder. ‘I don't want to murder him,' he said, and he suddenly went and murdered him. That's why they'll acquit him — because he struggled against it, and yet he murdered him.”
“But he didn't murder him,” Alyosha interrupted rather sharply. He was growing more and more sick with anxiety and impatience.
“Yes, I know — it was that old man Grigory who murdered him.”
“Grigory?” Alyosha cried.
“Yes, yes — it was Grigory. He was lying there where Dmitri Fyodorovitch had struck him down, and then he got up, saw the door open, went in, and killed Fyodor Pavlovitch.”
“But why, why?”

“Suffering from aberration. When he recovered from the blow Dmitri Fyodorovitch had given him on the head, he was suffering from aberration; he went and committed the murder. As for his saying he didn't, he very likely doesn't remember. Only, you know, it'll be better, ever so much better, if Dmitri Fyodorovitch murdered him. That's how it must have been, though I'm saying it was Grigory. It certainly was Dmitri Fyodorovitch, and that's better, ever so much better! Oh, not that a son should have killed his father — I don't defend that. Children ought to honor their parents — yet it would be better if it were he, because then you'd have nothing to cry about, since he did it while he was unconscious, or rather while he was conscious but didn't know what he was doing. Let them acquit him — that's so humane, and would show what a blessing the reformed courts are. I knew nothing about it, but they say this has been going on for a long time. And when I heard it yesterday I was so struck that I wanted to send for you at once. And if he's acquitted, make him come straight from the courthouse to dinner with me, and I'll have a party of friends, and we'll drink to the reformed courts. I don't believe he'd be dangerous; besides, I'll invite a great many people, so he could always be led out if he did anything. Then he might be made a justice of the peace or something in another town, because people who've been in trouble themselves make the best judges. And besides, who isn't suffering from aberration nowadays? — you, I, all of us are in a state of aberration, and there are ever so many examples of it: a man sits singing a song, something suddenly annoys him, he picks up a pistol and shoots the first person he comes across, and no one blames him for it. I read that recently, and all the doctors confirm it. The doctors are always confirming; they confirm anything. Why, my Lise is in a state of aberration. She made me cry again yesterday, and the day before too, and today I suddenly realized it's all down to aberration. Oh, Lise grieves me so! I believe she's quite mad. Why did she send for you? Did she send for you, or did you come on your own?”
“Yes, she sent for me, and I'm just going to her now.” Alyosha got up resolutely.

“Oh, my dear, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, perhaps this is the most important thing,” Madame Hohlakov cried, suddenly bursting into tears. “God knows I trust Lise to you with all my heart, and never mind her sending for you on the sly, without telling her mother. But forgive me, I can't trust my daughter so easily to your brother Ivan Fyodorovitch, though I still consider him the most chivalrous young man. But just imagine — he's been to see Lise, and I knew nothing about it!”
“How? What? When?” Alyosha was exceedingly surprised. He had not sat down again and was listening on his feet.

“I'll tell you; that's perhaps why I asked you to come — actually, I no longer know why I asked you to come. Well, Ivan Fyodorovitch has been to see me twice since he came back from Moscow. The first time he came as a friend to call on me, and the second time Katya was here and he came because he heard she was here. Of course, I didn't expect him to come often, knowing what a lot he has to do as it is, _vous comprenez, cette affaire et la mort terrible de votre papa_. But I suddenly heard he'd been here again — not to see me, but to see Lise. That's six days ago now. He came, stayed five minutes, and went away. And I didn't hear of it till three days afterwards, from Glafira, so it was a great shock to me. I sent for Lise directly. She laughed. ‘He thought you were asleep,' she said, ‘and came in to me to ask after your health.' Of course, that's how it happened. But Lise, Lise, mercy on us, how she distresses me! Would you believe it, one night, four days ago, right after you saw her last time and had gone away, she suddenly had a fit, screaming, shrieking, hysterics! Why is it I never have hysterics? Then the next day another fit, and the same thing on the third, and yesterday too, and then yesterday — that aberration. She suddenly screamed out, ‘I hate Ivan Fyodorovitch. I insist you never let him come to the house again.' I was struck dumb at these amazing words, and answered, ‘On what grounds could I refuse to see such an excellent young man, a young man of such learning too, and so unfortunate?' — because all this business is a misfortune, isn't it? She suddenly burst out laughing at my words, and so rudely, you know. Well, I was pleased; I thought I'd amused her and the fits would pass off, especially since I wanted to refuse to see Ivan Fyodorovitch anyway, on account of his strange visits without my knowledge, and I meant to ask him for an explanation. But early this morning Lise woke up and flew into a rage with Yulia and, would you believe it, slapped her in the face. That's monstrous; I'm always polite to my servants. And an hour later she was hugging Yulia's feet and kissing them. She sent a message to me that she wasn't coming to me at all, and would never come and see me again, and when I dragged myself down to her, she rushed to kiss me, crying, and as she kissed me, she pushed me out of the room without saying a word, so I couldn't find out what was the matter. Now, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, I rest all my hopes on you — my whole life is in your hands, in fact. I simply beg you to go to Lise and find out everything from her, as you alone can, and come back and tell me — me, her mother — because you understand it will be the death of me, simply the death of me, if this goes on, or else I shall run away. I can stand no more. I have patience; but I may lose patience, and then ... then something awful will happen. Ah, dear me! At last — Pyotr Ilyitch!” cried Madame Hohlakov, beaming all over as she saw Perhotin enter the room. “You are late, you are late! Well, sit down, speak, put us out of our suspense. What does the counsel say? Where are you off to, Alexey Fyodorovitch?”
“To Lise.”
“Oh, yes. You won't forget, you won't forget what I asked you? It's a question of life and death!”
“Of course I won't forget, if I can ... but I'm so late,” Alyosha muttered, beating a hasty retreat.
“No, be sure, be sure to come back in; don't say ‘if I can.' I'll die if you don't,” Madame Hohlakov called after him, but Alyosha had already left the room.
